title: Why the Postpandemic Tech Bust Sent Billionaires to Trump
gist: A book excerpt from Against Tech Oligarchy argues the 2022 rate shock — Fed funds from near zero to ~5.5 percent in 10 hikes over 15 months — destroyed roughly $4 trillion of combined market value across Amazon, Facebook, Apple, Google and Microsoft and triggered ~93,000 US tech layoffs in 2022 and 191,000 in 2023. The core mechanism: asset-light firms can cut engineers without near-term revenue loss because past labor is already congealed into codebases, so layoffs became a pure profitability lever that persisted long after the macro justification disappeared, while Biden-era antitrust and the internal tech-worker movement pushed newly radicalized billionaires toward Trump.

insights.claim: Between 2019 and 2022 Amazon grew headcount 92 percent and Facebook 93 percent, while Microsoft added nearly 80,000 employees and Google over 60,000 — a doubling of the largest workforces in the sector within three years.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline against which every subsequent 'efficiency' narrative is measured; headcount normalization was mechanical, not strategic insight.
insights.locator: Between 2019 and 2022, Amazon and Facebook more than doubled their head count

insights.claim: Large numbers of pandemic-era tech hires were onboarded to teams with no immediate tasks and held in reserve for projects that had not yet been planned — labor hoarding as an option on future growth.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Option-value hiring only pencils at zero rates; it identifies exactly which headcount is first to be cut when the discount rate rises.
insights.quote: they were, in other words, hired with nothing to do
insights.locator: With so many workers joining the industry, many were onboarded to teams

insights.claim: More than a decade of near-zero policy rates after the 2008 crisis made tech labor a prized asset, giving office workers skyrocketing salaries, unprecedented job mobility, and leverage to negotiate permanent remote work and project choice.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Tech worker bargaining power is a derivative of the rate environment, not of skill scarcity — the clearest single predictor of white-collar tech wage direction.
insights.locator: Tech’s pandemic-era hiring boom was underwritten by an extraordinary financial backdrop

insights.claim: The pandemic turned the tech sector from one powerful industry among many into the infrastructure underpinning every aspect of daily life, as Zoom, Slack and Microsoft Teams absorbed remote work, schooling, weddings, groceries and concerts.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Infrastructure status is what made the subsequent political backlash inevitable — utilities get regulated, platforms did not expect to be.
insights.locator: In the spring of 2020, as a new and highly contagious virus spread

themes.theme: The 2022 rate shock and the drawdown

insights.claim: The Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero to roughly 5.5 percent with 10 consecutive hikes in just 15 months, one of the most aggressive tightening campaigns in decades.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: The speed, not the level, is what broke long-duration business models; watch hike cadence rather than terminal rate when modeling growth-equity stress.
insights.locator: Then inflation hit as an unprecedented flood of pandemic-era stimulus cash

insights.claim: In 2022 the S&P 500 fell 19.4 percent — its largest drop since 2008 — while the tech industry fell 30 percent, its third-worst year ever after 2008 and the 2000 dot-com bust.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Quantifies tech's beta to rates at roughly 1.5x the index in a tightening shock — a reusable stress-test parameter.
insights.locator: The S&P 500 fell 19.4 percent, the largest drop since 2008

insights.claim: Almost $4 trillion in combined market value vanished from Amazon, Facebook, Apple, Google and Microsoft, with Facebook losing two-thirds of its value, Amazon half, and nearly $1 trillion shaved off Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Megacap concentration means a rate shock transmits to index investors through five names — the same concentration risk that exists today.
insights.locator: Almost $4 trillion in combined market value vanished

insights.claim: The 2022 fundamental deterioration was specific and identifiable: sluggish Amazon growth with razor-thin margins, four consecutive quarterly profit declines at Google on digital ad weakness, and decelerating Microsoft cloud growth.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Ad spend and cloud growth rates are the two megacap early-warning indicators; both turned before the multiple compressed.
insights.locator: Major tech firms began missing Wall Street’s expectations

insights.claim: High rates hit tech hardest because the opportunity cost of risky bets rises when cash earns a real return, pushing investors from long-shot future-monopoly promises toward safer, more predictable outcomes.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: The monopoly-optionality valuation framework only works below a rate threshold; above it, the narrative premium disappears regardless of execution.
insights.locator: So why was tech hit so hard?

insights.claim: The tech industry's self-presentation flipped from frontier of unstoppable growth to austerity almost in lockstep with the Fed's hikes, showing corporate narrative is downstream of monetary policy rather than of strategy.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Treat management 'discipline' messaging as a rate-regime indicator, not as new information about business quality.
insights.locator: Almost in lockstep with the Fed’s unprecedented interest rate hikes

themes.theme: Why layoffs pay in asset-light firms

insights.claim: In asset-light firms with no capital tied up in facilities or merchandise, labor is the largest cost and the easiest line item to cut — the structural reason tech absorbs macro shocks through headcount rather than capex.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Predicts where the adjustment lands in any software-sector downturn: payroll first, everything else second.
insights.locator: For asset-light tech firms, where capital isn’t tied up in facilities

insights.claim: Cutting tech workers does not immediately reduce revenue because the value of their past labor is already congealed into the codebases running automated digital products, so layoffs boost profitability without short-term penalty — the reverse of a traditional firm.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: The single most important mechanism in the piece: it explains why tech layoffs are self-reinforcing and why the damage shows up only in deferred product decay, years later.
insights.locator: Because of this, laying off tech workers does not result in an immediate loss of revenue

insights.claim: Every layoff announcement triggered a stock bump — Facebook's first major round sent shares up 5 percent overnight — making job cuts a reliable lever for stimulating investor confidence independent of operational need.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: A direct tradeable reflex: layoff announcements in asset-light tech are a repeatable short-term positive catalyst regardless of underlying fundamentals.
insights.locator: Every layoff announcement triggered a bump in stock price

insights.claim: US tech layoffs hit nearly 93,000 in 2022 and accelerated to over 191,000 in 2023, with Facebook cutting 11,000 (over 10 percent of staff), Amazon 10,000 corporate roles, Google and Microsoft over 10,000 each, and Twitter shedding 80 percent of staff under Elon Musk.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Twitter's 80 percent cut without immediate collapse became the proof-of-concept that emboldened the rest of the sector to cut deeper.
insights.locator: At the end of 2022, Facebook cut 11,000 jobs

insights.claim: Austerity measures introduced as a temporary macro correction outlived the conditions that justified them and hardened into a permanent managerial strategy, persisting after the Fed engineered a soft landing with inflation falling from 9 percent to 3 percent by mid-2023 and megacap earnings beating expectations.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Do not expect tech hiring or comp to mean-revert with rates; the labor regime shift is structural, which supports sustained margin expansion.
insights.locator: What began as a financial response to a deteriorating macroeconomic outlook

insights.claim: The release of OpenAI's ChatGPT injected fresh boosterism and a massive infusion of new capital into the sector even as layoffs continued, letting firms run austerity and an investment boom simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Explains the apparent paradox of record capex alongside record layoffs — capital rotated from headcount to compute, not out of the sector.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT injected a new jolt

insights.claim: New computer science graduates faced their worst year since the dot-com bust in 2023, with qualified candidates unable to secure a single interview after hundreds of applications.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Entry-level collapse feeds forward into a mid-career talent gap five to ten years out, and into the political economy of tech backlash now.
insights.locator: In 2023, new computer science grads faced their worst year

themes.theme: The 'fake work' narrative as ideological groundwork

insights.claim: Rather than acknowledge their own reckless expansion, tech CEOs and venture capitalists redirected blame onto workers, laying the ideological groundwork for mass layoffs before the layoffs began.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: A recognizable pre-cut tell: when leadership language shifts to worker productivity, the restructuring is already decided.
insights.locator: But rather than acknowledge their own reckless expansion

insights.claim: Silicon Valley investor Keith Rabois publicly declared that thousands of Facebook and Google employees were doing 'fake work' and simply sat at their desks doing nothing.
insights.speaker: Keith Rabois
insights.so_what: Elite investor rhetoric legitimized deep cuts across the sector; these statements front-ran the actual announcements.
insights.quote: sit at their desks and do nothing
insights.locator: Silicon Valley investor Keith Rabois, a prominent voice among tech elites

insights.claim: Andreessen Horowitz general partner David Ulevitch suggested as much as half of Google's white-collar workforce was not contributing meaningful labor, attributing it to the rise of 'bullshit jobs' filling head count rather than delivering results.
insights.speaker: David Ulevitch
insights.so_what: If a top-tier VC publicly believes half a megacap's white-collar staff is redundant, margin expectations for the sector reset permanently higher.
insights.locator: David Ulevitch, a general partner at the prestigious venture capital firm

insights.claim: Sundar Pichai told a 2022 all-hands that productivity as a whole was not where it needed to be, Wayfair's Niraj Shah warned employees that laziness is not rewarded with success, and Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'year of efficiency' — a coordinated executive rhetoric shift across firms.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Synchronized messaging across unrelated companies signals sector-wide margin repair, not idiosyncratic company problems — a broad long signal on tech margins.
insights.quote: there is not a lot of history of laziness being rewarded with success
insights.locator: Tech CEOs also piled on.

insights.claim: Marc Andreessen framed tech employees as the 'laptop class' — Western upper-middle-class professionals working through a screen and abstracted from tangible physical reality — before mass layoffs began.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: The framing that made cutting knowledge workers morally comfortable; the same rhetoric now underwrites AI-driven replacement of white-collar roles.
insights.quote: Western upper-middle-class professionals who work through a screen and are totally abstracted from tangible physical reality
insights.locator: Even before mass layoffs began, Andreessen was eager to frame tech workers

themes.theme: Techlash, antitrust and the Democratic rupture

insights.claim: The populist left — Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — made breaking up Big Tech core political messaging, converting the industry from liberal America's darling into a symbol of corporate excess.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk premium for platforms became bipartisan; neither party is now a reliable protector of platform incumbency.
insights.locator: This backlash gave new momentum to a rising populist left

insights.claim: The Biden administration was the most tech-skeptical Democratic government in decades: FTC chair Lina Khan launched sweeping antitrust suits against Amazon and Facebook, the SEC and Treasury cracked down on crypto and sent valuations plummeting, and AI was framed as needing federal oversight.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Establishes the policy baseline against which any current deregulatory shift is measured — the crypto and AI regime swings are the asset-price transmission channel.
insights.locator: Under Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan

insights.claim: Personal exclusion mattered as much as policy: Elon Musk was left out of Biden's 2021 electric vehicles summit that included GM, Ford and Chrysler but not Tesla, and Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz complained of being unable to get meetings with senior officials.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Access, not tax or regulation alone, flipped the largest political donors in the sector — a low-cost variable that policymakers repeatedly underweight.
insights.locator: Many of Silicon Valley’s top figures also felt personally snubbed

insights.claim: Right-wing ideology inside tech predates the 2022 bust: Peter Thiel had openly declared freedom and democracy incompatible and allied with Trump in 2016, while Curtis Yarvin's 'techno-monarchism' had already forged ties to JD Vance.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: The intellectual scaffolding existed in advance; the bust supplied the constituency, which is why the political realignment was fast and durable rather than opportunistic.
insights.locator: The conservative ideas underpinning Trump’s following are not entirely new

insights.claim: Tech worker organizing escalated from isolated dissent over military contracts, Big Oil partnerships and harassment into formal unions — the first wall-to-wall union at Kickstarter and the Alphabet Workers Union, backed by the Communication Workers of America and OPEIU.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Union infrastructure now exists in the sector even if membership is small; it is the vehicle any future downturn-driven labor response will use.
insights.locator: They’ve also started to organize—from the first wall-to-wall union at Kickstarter

insights.claim: Marc Andreessen explicitly linked his own political radicalization to the tech worker movement, saying companies were being hijacked into engines of social revolution and that firms he knew felt hours away from violent riots on their own campuses by their own employees.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Names the actual trigger for the capital-side political shift: internal labor pressure, not taxes or antitrust — so worker militancy is now a political-risk variable for portfolio companies.
insights.locator: Andreessen explicitly linked his own radicalization

insights.claim: A generation of Silicon Valley executives were apolitical technocrats taught that progressivism and capitalism were mutually reinforcing and that wealth proved moral virtue, and the techlash shattered that illusion, producing a reactionary break with the old Californian Ideology.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Explains why the shift is ideological and sticky rather than transactional — expect sustained political spending from tech capital regardless of who is in office.
insights.locator: Out of this disillusionment emerged a new billionaire consciousness

insights.claim: Worker autonomy, once celebrated as the key to creativity and innovation, was recast as indulgence and weakness, converting the management-worker relationship from a common mission into an openly declared power struggle.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Cultural perks and autonomy are gone as a cost line and as a recruiting moat — a structural margin tailwind and a long-run innovation question.
insights.locator: Where worker autonomy had once been celebrated as a key to creativity

insights.claim: Tech billionaires backed Trump both to win a culture war against the left-liberal foundations they blamed for turning workers against them and to avoid another round of Biden-style regulation, forming a power bloc uniting capital and politics around restoring control.
insights.speaker: Js Tan
insights.so_what: Frames the tech-Trump alliance as a durable defensive arrangement over labor and regulation, implying policy capture rather than a cyclical donor rotation.
insights.locator: And so, these billionaires set their sights on winning the culture war
